claims.statement: Inuktitut is written in Nunavut with a syllabic script called qaniujaaqpait. Each consonant has one character, and that character is rotated or reversed to show the three vowels i, u and a. A long vowel is marked with a dot placed above the character. When a consonant is not followed by a vowel, a smaller raised character called a final (naniq, plural naniit) is used. Confirmed character values: ᒥ mi, ᒧ mu, ᒪ ma, ᐃ i, ᐅ u, ᐊ a.

sources.ref: Inuktut Tusaalanga (Pirurvik Centre, funded by the Government of Nunavut) — How to read syllabics
Inuktut Tusaalanga — Writing the Inuit Language (qaniujaaqpait / qaliujaaqpait, ICI orthography)
Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami — Inuktut Qaliujaaqpait project (1976 common writing system effort; two forms)

claims.statement: The floe edge is the boundary where land-fast ice meets open water. It is called sinaa in Inuktitut. Seals, polar bears, walrus, narwhal, bowhead and beluga whales and many birds gather there, which is why it has long been a place Inuit travel to.

claims.statement: The older runic alphabet had 24 characters. By the beginning of the Viking Age it had been reduced to 16. In the 16-character alphabet one character served several sounds: the t rune stood for both t and d, the k rune for both k and g, and the u rune for u, o, y and ø.

By the beginning of the Viking Age it had been modified and comprised 16 characters… the rune t represented both t and d, the rune k represented k and g')
Historiska museet — Runes (history hub): 'The common Viking-Age runic alphabet had 16 characters, developed from earlier alphabets with more signs.'

claims.statement: Two royal rune stones stand at Jelling in Jutland. King Gorm the Old raised the smaller stone for his wife Thyra; its inscription reads 'King Gorm made this monument to his wife Thyra, Denmark's ornament'. Around 965 King Harald Bluetooth raised the larger stone in memory of his parents Gorm and Thyra. Denmark is named on the larger stone, which is why it is often called Denmark's birth certificate.

claims.statement: Most Viking-Age rune stones are memorials raised by relatives, and they follow a standard formula: X had this stone raised in memory of Y, his or her named relation. Museum examples: 'Ragnvaldr had the runes carved in memory of Fastvé, his mother' and 'Þorsteinn had the landmark made in memory of Sveinn, his father.'

claims.statement: Four English weekday names carry Germanic god names: Tuesday from Tiw (Old English name for Týr), Wednesday from Woden (the Old English form of Odin), Thursday from Thunor/Thor, and Friday from Frige (Old Norse Frigg). Saturday, Sunday and Monday do not: they keep Saturn, the Sun and the Moon.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Week (origin of the English day-names; Germanic deities substituted for Roman ones)

claims.statement: In Gylfaginning the fetter Gleipnir is made of six things: the noise a cat makes when it walks, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. The list is the story's explanation for why those six things cannot be found in the world.

claims.statement: In Skáldskaparmál six treasures are made by two groups of dwarfs. The sons of Ivaldi make Sif's golden hair, the ship Skidbladnir and the spear Gungnir. Brokk and his brother Sindri make the boar Gullinbursti, the ring Draupnir and the hammer Mjollnir. The treasures are then given out: Odin receives Gungnir and Draupnir, Thor receives Mjollnir, Freyr receives Skidbladnir and Gullinbursti, and Sif receives the hair.

claims.statement: In Skáldskaparmál the order of the Idun episode is fixed by the text: Loki is caught by the eagle Thjazi and buys his freedom with a promise; Loki lures Idun out of Asgard with her apples; Thjazi carries her away; the gods grow old and grey; the gods force Loki to bring her back; Loki carries her home in the shape of a nut and Thjazi, chasing as an eagle, is burned at the walls of Asgard.

claims.statement: The keel and the stems form the backbone of a Viking ship. The hull is clinker-built: each strake overlaps the one below it and the strakes are fixed with iron rivets; the Oseberg ship's hull has twelve strakes a side. The ship is steered with a side rudder mounted on the right-hand side, and the English word starboard comes from Old Norse styrbord, the side where you steer.

claims.statement: The Kalevala gives the kantele two origins: the first kantele is made from the jaw of a giant pike and strung with horsehair, and a second one is made of birch. Real kanteles have been built with different numbers of strings (5, 8, 10, 12 and, in modern concert forms, 39), and older ones were carved from a single piece of wood before builders began using planks about three hundred years ago.

claims.statement: The Kalevala was compiled by Elias Lonnrot, a doctor and folklore collector, from oral poems that had been passed down in Karelia and eastern Finland. He travelled from village to village recording verses, then combined and edited them into one long poem. The first Kalevala appeared in 1835 with 32 poems, and an enlarged edition appeared in 1849 with 50 poems.

claims.statement: The Kalevala is written in an unrhymed four-beat trochaic line known as the Kalevala metre, and its style is characterised by alliteration, parallelism and repetition. Alliteration in this verse binds words inside a line by their opening sounds, not by rhyme at the line ends.

claims.statement: Finnish has eight vowels in three groups: front (a-umlaut, o-umlaut, y), back (a, o, u) and neutral (e, i). Front and back vowels do not occur together inside one simple word; the neutral vowels e and i occur with either group.

claims.statement: Ogham is the earliest written form of the Irish language. Its original alphabet has twenty letters arranged in four groups of five, called aicmi. The letters are cut as notches and strokes on, across or either side of a central stem line, usually the edge of a standing stone, and are read from the bottom upward. Ogham stones date from about the fourth to the sixth century AD and usually record a person's name in a set formula such as X son of Y, of the tribe of Z; the formula word MAQI means 'son of'.

sources.ref: Heritage Ireland / Office of Public Works — Ballintaggart Ogham Stones ('The ogham alphabet uses a script made of lines cut on, across, or either side of, a central stem line. Ogham inscriptions were usually written vertically and are read from bottom to top… usually record the name of a person with a standard formula such as: X son of Y, member of the tribe of Z')

claims.statement: In the tale of the fate of the children of Lir the four children spend nine hundred years as swans, in three spans of three hundred years each and in three named waters, in this order: Lough Derravaragh, then the Sea of Moyle between Ireland and Scotland, then Erris (Iorrus Domhnann) in the west.

sources.ref: CELT: Corpus of Electronic Texts, University College Cork — 'The Fate of the Children of Lir' (three hundred years on Lough Derravaragh, three hundred on the Sea of Moyle, three hundred at Iorrus Domhnann)
Heritage Ireland / Office of Public Works — Women, Water and Wisdom in Celtic Mythology (four children cursed to live 900 years as swans)
dúchas.ie — The Schools' Collection, National Folklore Collection, University College Dublin (Westmeath Lake; the children of Lir on Lough Derravaragh)
